title: The World of the Last Ice Age
objective: After this level you can describe what the planet looked like about 20,000 years ago, when ice sheets covered much of North America.
summary: Twenty thousand years ago Earth was about 6 °C colder, with ice over North America to Wisconsin. The world was dry and dusty, and grinding ice left loess that now makes fertile soil.

cards.headline: At the peak of the last ice age, Earth was only about 6 °C colder than today.
cards.body: That was enough to push ice sheets as far south as Wisconsin. As paleoclimatologist Jessica Tierney put it, that is 'a huge change.'

cards.headline: A frozen north
cards.body: About 20,000 years ago, at the Last Glacial Maximum, Earth's average temperature was about 8 °C. You met the lower seas and the Bering land bridge in World Geography. Here's more of the picture: the Laurentide, Cordilleran and Greenland ice sheets spread across North America, reaching as far south as Wisconsin.

cards.headline: Dry, dusty and low on carbon
cards.body: An ice-age world wasn't just colder; it was drier. Less moisture meant fewer plants and bigger deserts, and dust filled the air. Carbon dioxide sank as low as about 180 parts per million.

cards.headline: Ice-age dust you can farm
cards.body: Grinding ice sheets crushed rock into fine powder, and winds carried the silt far away as loess. Loess now covers about 10% of Earth's land, including plains along the Mississippi and Missouri valleys. It carries quartz and feldspar, Chapter 1's old friends, and the soils that form on it are typically fertile and good for intensive farming.

cards.headline: Ice-age world: pictured
learned: The ice age was about 6 °C colder

questions.prompt: At the peak of the last ice age, Earth's average temperature was _____ colder than today.

options.label: About 0.5 °C
options.rationale: That is closer to a big eruption's dip.

options.label: About 20 °C
options.rationale: The real difference was much smaller.

options.label: About 60 °C
options.rationale: That would freeze the whole planet solid.

questions.explanation: The Last Glacial Maximum was about 6 °C colder on average, which was enough for ice to reach Wisconsin.

questions.prompt: Match each with its figure from the last ice age and after.
questions.explanation: At the Last Glacial Maximum, Earth's average temperature was about 8 °C and carbon dioxide sank to about 180 ppm. Loess now covers about 10% of Earth's land.

questions.prompt: A soil develops as its parent material weathers. For many soils along the Mississippi valley, what is that parent material?

options.label: Windblown silt ground up by ice sheets
Fresh lava from recent eruptions
options.rationale: There are no active volcanoes there.

options.label: Solid granite bedrock right at the surface
options.rationale: Their parent material is windblown silt, not bedrock.

options.label: Coral reefs from a warm shallow sea
options.rationale: It's ice-age dust, not old reefs.

questions.explanation: Loess, silt ground fine by ice sheets and spread by the wind, blankets the Mississippi and Missouri valleys and weathers into fertile soil.
